## Main projects

### 2024.01 to 2024.12 · Sampletown First Hospital fever clinic mini program

A mini program that lets a patient with a fever book a slot, answer the triage questions at home and see the queue. Alex designed the booking flow and the triage form, and tested both with nurses on the ward. Waiting time at the clinic door fell from 40 minutes to 12 in the first quarter after launch.

What Alex did:

- Interviewed eleven nurses and six patients in the first two weeks, and sat at the clinic desk for three morning shifts to see where the queue broke down.
- Cut the triage form from 23 questions to 9 by asking the clinic's lead doctor which answers ever changed where a patient was sent.
- Designed the slot picker so that a patient who is too unwell to read much can book with three taps, and a family member can book for them.
- Wrote the messages a patient gets when a slot moves, in plain words, and had them checked by the ward's head nurse.
- Ran two rounds of testing with printed screens before any code was written, and one round on a test build with twenty patients.
- Handed over a specification of 34 screens with every empty, loading and failed state drawn.

The clinic kept the paper queue for the first month beside the mini program. By the third month nine patients in ten arrived with a slot already booked, and the clinic stopped printing queue tickets.

### 2023.05 to 2024.12 · Example Hospital customer management platform and doctor assistant app

A platform where the hospital's service team keeps each patient's contact history, and an app that shows a doctor the day's patients and their notes. Alex designed both and the hand-over between them. The doctor assistant app is used by 180 doctors every working day.

What Alex did:

- Mapped how a patient's question travelled between the call centre, the service desk and the ward before the platform existed: seven hand-overs on average, three of them on paper.
- Designed the patient timeline, which puts calls, visits, messages and follow-up tasks in one list that the whole service team reads.
- Designed the doctor's day view around the ward round: who is next, what changed since yesterday, and what the service team promised the patient.
- Set the rule that a note written in the app shows on the platform within a minute, and drew what each side sees while it waits.
- Worked with two engineers on an offline mode for the wards in the old building, where the signal drops.
- Trained the service team's four leads, who then trained the other forty people.

The service team now answers a returning patient without asking them to repeat their history. The hospital extended the app from two departments to all nine after the first half year.

### 2022.06 to 2023.04 · Example District epidemic data dashboard

A wall-sized dashboard for the district's health office that shows cases, beds and supplies by street. Alex designed the layout and the colour scale, and wrote the rules for what the screen shows when a data feed is late. The office used it in its daily briefing for ten months.

What Alex did:

- Sat in on the office's morning briefing for two weeks to learn which five numbers the director asked for first.
- Designed a map of the district's 46 streets with one colour scale that still reads from the back of the room and for people who can't tell red from green.
- Drew the bed and supply panels so that a shortage shows as a count of days left, not as a percentage.
- Wrote the stale-data rules: a figure older than six hours turns grey and says when it was last updated.
- Built a click-through prototype on the real wall screen, and changed the type sizes twice after standing at the back of the room.
- Agreed with the data team which figures the screen must never estimate.

The director stopped asking for a printed summary after the second week. When the office closed its daily briefing, it kept the dashboard for the weekly one.

### 2020.09 to 2022.02 · Example Group management cockpit back office

A back office where the group's managers see revenue, costs and headcount for each of its 14 companies. Alex designed the cockpit's pages and the drill-down from a group figure to a company's own. It replaced a monthly spreadsheet that took the finance team three days to build.

What Alex did:

- Collected the 31 spreadsheets the finance team stitched together each month and listed which figures appeared in more than one with different values.
- Agreed one definition for each of the 18 figures with the finance director before drawing a page.
- Designed the group page, the company page and the path between them, so that a manager can go from a group figure to the company that moved it in two clicks.
- Designed the monthly close view, which shows which companies have sent their numbers and which are late.
- Added a note field beside each figure so that a company's finance lead can explain a jump once, where everyone reads it.
- Ran the old spreadsheet and the cockpit side by side for three month-ends and listed every difference.

After the third month-end the finance team stopped building the spreadsheet. The group's board pack now takes its figures from the cockpit's export.

### 2018.10 to 2019.06 · Example Exchange cross-chain data platform

A data platform that shows transfers between four blockchains in one place for the exchange's risk team. Alex designed the transfer explorer and the alert rules screen. The risk team's daily check went from two hours to twenty minutes.

What Alex did:

- Shadowed the risk team's two analysts for a week and wrote down each lookup they did by hand in four separate block explorers.
- Designed the transfer explorer: one search box that takes an address or a transaction from any of the four chains and shows where the funds went next.
- Designed the alert rules screen, where an analyst sets a threshold in plain terms and sees how often it would have fired last month.
- Drew the path view, which follows funds across a bridge and marks each hop with its chain and its time.
- Wrote the interaction specification of 52 pages that the six engineers built from.
- Tested the explorer with both analysts on last quarter's real cases before launch.

The analysts closed the four block explorers they kept open all day. Two alerts in the first month caught transfers that the manual check had missed the quarter before.

### 2017.08 to 2018.09 · Example Bond Link back office

A back office for a bond trading link that runs on a permissioned blockchain, where operations staff match and settle the day's trades. Alex designed the matching screen and the exceptions queue. It handled about 900 trades a day at launch.

What Alex did:

- Learned the settlement day from the operations lead: when trades arrive, when they must match, and what happens to one that doesn't.
- Designed the matching screen as two lists side by side, with the fields that disagree marked, so that a mismatch is seen without reading every field.
- Designed the exceptions queue, ordered by how soon each trade must settle, with the reason each one is there.
- Added keyboard shortcuts for the five actions the staff do hundreds of times a day, after timing the mouse-only prototype.
- Drew the end-of-day report that the operations lead signs.
- Stayed on the operations floor for the first two weeks after launch and fixed eleven small problems.

The team of five settled the first month's trades with no late settlement. The exceptions queue became the first screen each of them opens in the morning.
